id: ‘One morn I left him in his bed’

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

One morn I left him in his bed; A moment after some one said, ‘Your child is dying – he is dead.’ We made him ready for his rest, Flowers in his hair, and on his breast His little hands together prest. We sailed by night across the sea; So, floating from the world were we, Apart from sympathy, we Three. The wild sea moaned, the black clouds spread Moving shadows on its bed, But one of us lay midship dead. I saw his coffin sliding down The yellow sand in yonder town, Where I put on my sorrow’s crown. Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker’s child suddenly dies after being left in bed one morning.
- The child is lovingly prepared for burial with flowers and folded hands.
- The family carries the child’s body across the sea at night, isolated in their grief.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem confronts the death of a child and the speaker’s bereavement through a first-person elegiac recollection of the child’s preparation, sea journey, burial, and return home. It reveals grief as overwhelming and isolating, showing that such loss becomes an entire universe for mourning parents.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, Your, Flowers

outputs.L1:
One morning, I left him in his bed;  
A moment later, someone said,  
“Your child is dying—he is dead.”

We prepared him for his rest,  
With flowers in his hair, and on his breast  
His little hands together pressed.

We sailed by night across the sea;  
Thus, drifting from the world, were we,  
Apart from sympathy—we three.

The wild sea moaned; the black clouds spread  
Their moving shadows on its bed,  
While one of us lay midship, dead.

I saw his coffin sliding down  
The yellow sand in that distant town,  
Where I put on my sorrow’s crown.

And we returned; in this drear place,  
Never to see him face to face,  
I thrust aside the living race.

Mothers who mourn with me today,  
Oh, understand me when I say:  
I cannot weep; I cannot pray.

I gaze upon a hidden store—  
His books, his toys, the clothes he wore—  
And cry, “Once more—to me, once more!”

Then take from me this simple verse,  
That you may know what I rehearse:  
A grief—yours and mine—the Universe.
outputs.L2:
One morning, I left him lying in bed.  
Soon afterward, someone came and told me,  
“Your child is dying—he is gone.”

We prepared him for his final sleep,  
placing flowers in his hair,  
and folding his small hands upon his chest.

That night we crossed the sea by boat,  
as though we were drifting away from the world,  
cut off from all comfort—just the three of us.

The restless ocean groaned,  
dark clouds cast shifting shadows over the water,  
and one among us lay dead in the middle of the ship.

I watched his coffin being lowered  
into the yellow sand of that distant town,  
and there I took upon myself the weight of grief.

Then we came back. In this bleak place,  
where I will never again see his face,  
I turned away from the living world.

Mothers who grieve as I do today,  
please understand me when I tell you:  
I cannot cry, and I cannot pray.

I look at the treasured things kept out of sight—  
his books, his playthings, the clothes he once wore—  
and I plead, “Give him back to me, just once more!”

So accept these plain lines from me,  
so that you may know the sorrow I speak of:  
a grief that is both yours and mine—our whole universe.
outputs.L3:
One morning, the speaker leaves her child resting in bed, never imagining that anything is wrong. But suddenly and unexpectedly, the child dies. What had begun as an ordinary day is transformed into a moment of devastating loss, and the family is left stunned by the child’s death.

The child’s body is then tenderly prepared for burial. Loved ones arrange flowers around the child and fold the small hands gently, treating the body with care, reverence, and affection. These quiet actions show the depth of the family’s love and their desire to honor the child even in death.

At night, the family carries the child’s body across the sea. The journey is dark, silent, and lonely, emphasizing their isolation in grief. Surrounded by the vastness of the water and the darkness of night, they are separated from the rest of the world, enclosed in their sorrow as they bear the child away.

After reaching a distant town, they bury the child. The burial marks the final separation, and the speaker must return home without the child. This return is filled with unbearable sadness. The home that once held the child’s presence now feels empty, and the speaker is overwhelmed by the weight of loss.

In the end, the speaker turns to other mothers who have also known grief. She speaks to them as someone who understands the deepest kind of suffering. Her sorrow is so intense that she cannot even cry or pray. The grief has gone beyond ordinary expression, leaving her numb, silent, and unable to find comfort.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the death of a child through a deeply personal, first-person elegiac recollection. The speaker looks back on the painful sequence of events surrounding the child’s death: the child’s body is prepared, taken on a sea journey, buried, and then remembered as the mourning parent returns home. By tracing these stages, the poem does not treat death as a single moment, but as a devastating process that the bereaved must endure step by step. Each action becomes charged with sorrow, and ordinary details are transformed into reminders of loss.

The speaker’s grief is shown as overwhelming and isolating. The death of the child separates the parent from the normal world, making everything feel altered by bereavement. The sea journey and burial suggest both physical distance and emotional separation, while the return home intensifies the absence of the child. Home, which should be a place of comfort and family life, becomes marked by emptiness. Through this movement away from and back to familiar places, the poem reveals how grief follows the speaker everywhere.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that the loss of a child is not simply one sorrow among many, but a complete world of suffering for the parents. Their grief becomes all-encompassing, shaping their memories, surroundings, and sense of reality. The poem’s first-person voice makes this mourning intimate and immediate, allowing the reader to feel the depth of the speaker’s bereavement. In doing so, it portrays parental loss as a grief so profound that it becomes an entire universe of pain, memory, and love.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Victorian-style elegiac poem from the perspective of a grieving mother whose young child dies suddenly, is carried by sea for burial, and leaves her unable to pray or weep.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Little Coffin at Sea**

They laid thee where the lilies failed,  
My little one, my snow-white dove;  
So still the morning watched and paled,  
So hushed the house that learned my love.  
No fever-flush upon thy cheek,  
No long farewell thy lips could keep—  
One cry, one breath too faint to speak,  
And thou wert in that deeper sleep.

I smoothed the curls upon thy brow,  
I set thy folded hands aright;  
Ah me! I know not clearly how  
The sun went down, or came the night.  
They whispered comfort near my chair,  
They read of mansions in the skies;  
I heard the words hang cold in air,  
And could not lift to God mine eyes.

Then over waters grey and wide  
They bore thee from thy mother’s door;  
The slow ship moved against the tide,  
And left me standing on the shore.  
O bitter was the salt sea-wind,  
O black the gulls that wheeled above;  
I watched till sight itself grew blind,  
And all the world went out with love.

Thou hadst not feared the waves before,  
My babe, when shells were in thy hand;  
Thou laughedst at the murmuring shore,  
And chased the foam along the sand.  
But now the deep, with solemn breast,  
Received thee in its mournful care,  
To bear thee to thy narrow rest,  
And I—I had no tears, no prayer.

They tell me Heaven is very fair,  
That little children walk in white;  
That seraphs braid thy golden hair,  
And keep thee in the Lord’s own light.  
I know the texts, I know the creed,  
The sacred promises they say;  
Yet in my heart is but a reed  
The tempest breaks and casts away.

For prayer is frozen on my tongue,  
And weeping with my life is fled;  
The songs my mother o’er me sung  
Lie dumb beside thy little bed.  
I kneel, but Heaven is far and dim;  
I clasp my hands, but cannot cry;  
My soul goes wandering after him  
Who sailed beneath the leaden sky.

Come back in dreams, if dreams may cross  
The waters and the churchyard stone;  
Come as thou wert before my loss,  
And let me hear thy voice, mine own.  
Call “Mother” once from that far strand  
Where all my hopes lie cold and deep—  
So may I feel thy vanished hand,  
And learn at last to pray—or weep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a mournful narrative poem in rhyming tercets about parents losing their child, preparing his body with flowers, sailing across a stormy sea with the coffin, and returning home to his toys and clothes.
counterfactuals.output:
They found him where the morning lost its light,  
A little hand grown still as winter’s white,  
And all the house bent inward from the night.  

His mother washed his brow with trembling care,  
His father combed the gold out of his hair,  
And laid small blossoms softly everywhere.  

They tucked white lilies near his quiet head,  
And roses at the feet that would not tread,  
Then kissed the cheek no lullaby could red.  

The coffin waited, narrow, pale, and deep,  
A cradle built for silence and for sleep;  
They closed it while the rafters seemed to weep.  

At dusk they bore him down the harbor stones,  
Past gulls that cried like lost and broken tones,  
Past nets, past lamps, past waves like grinding bones.  

The sea rose black; the mast began to moan,  
The rain beat hard as fists on wood and stone,  
And still they held the box that held their own.  

His mother prayed against the thunder’s roar,  
His father stared toward an unseen shore,  
As if one breath might bring him back once more.  

The lantern swung; the salt wind lashed their eyes,  
The coffin shone beneath the storm-torn skies,  
A little star no tempest could revise.  

All night the vessel climbed each shattered wave,  
All night they kept their vigil, worn and brave,  
And would have traded breath to be his grave.  

At dawn the storm lay broken, spent, and gray;  
They turned the boat and brought him home by day,  
With petals bruised but not yet blown away.  

They crossed the threshold neither spoke his name;  
The hearth was cold, the rooms were just the same,  
Yet nothing there could ever be the same.  

His wooden horse stood waiting by the chair,  
His soldiers guarded kingdoms in the air,  
His kite lay folded, longing for repair.  

Small boots still leaned beside the garden door,  
A shirt hung blue upon the nursery floor,  
And one sock slept where he had slept before.  

His mother held the coat he used to wear,  
And pressed her face into its empty air,  
As if his warmth were still imprisoned there.  

His father wound the toy train round its track;  
It clicked ahead, it faltered, circled back,  
Then stopped beside a tunnel painted black.  

So evening filled the house with ash and rain,  
With tiny sleeves, with cups he’d use again,  
With all the shapes of love remade as pain.  

And in the room where once his laughter grew,  
They sat among the flowers, pale and few,  
Two hearts still beating where the storm passed through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a 19th-century sentimental poem on bereavement, using archaic diction and regular rhyme, ending with a direct address to other mourning mothers.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Empty Cradle**

The twilight falleth soft and gray,  
The hearth is dim and lone;  
My little lamb hath gone away,  
And I am left to moan.  

His tiny shoes beside the door  
Await his step in vain;  
His voice shall fill the rooms no more  
With music after rain.  

O cruel hush! O vacant chair!  
O pillow white and cold!  
I smooth again his silken hair  
In dreams I cannot hold.  

They tell me he is gone above,  
Where fadeless lilies blow,  
And angels bear him in their love  
Where sin may never go.  

Yet still I stretch mine arms at night,  
And call his cherished name,  
But only shadows, pale and slight,  
Creep round the dying flame.  

The spring shall robe the fields in green,  
The birds shall sing full sweet;  
But never shall my eyes have seen  
His dancing, dimpled feet.  

Ah, Lord, if tears may reach Thy throne,  
Receive this broken cry;  
Thou gav’st the blossom as mine own,  
Then took’st it to the sky.  

Sleep, darling, in thy narrow bed,  
Beneath the churchyard sod;  
The roses whisper o’er thy head,  
Thy soul is safe with God.  

And when my weary day is done,  
And death unbars the door,  
Lead me, my lost, my little one,  
To clasp thee evermore.  

O mourning mothers, bowed and mild,  
Who weep when none may see,  
God keep each dear departed child—  
And comfort you and me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tragic first-person poem about the death and burial of a little boy, including images of his folded hands, a nighttime sea voyage, yellow sand, and the speaker’s overwhelming grief.
counterfactuals.output:
I laid his little hands across his chest,  
two folded birds that would not rise again,  
and smoothed the hair from off his cooling brow  
as if my touch could call him back from sleep.  

The room grew still around his smallest breath  
gone out like candlelight beneath a door;  
I called his name until my voice was ash,  
until the walls had learned my grief by heart.  

That night we took him over the dark sea,  
the moon a broken coin upon the waves,  
the boat creaking softly under sorrow,  
and black water closing round our wake.  

No gull cried out. No star seemed kind.  
I held the shroud and felt the world fall wide—  
too vast, too empty, endless as the tide,  
with my poor heart beating on alone.  

At dawn we came to the yellow sand,  
where small shells shone like tears beside our feet.  
They dug a bed for him above the shore,  
so near the sea he loved, so far from me.  

I watched them lower all my sunlight down,  
his folded hands hidden under linen,  
his face turned from the morning and my kiss,  
his silence heavier than any earth.  

O little boy, my joy, my briefest spring,  
the spade struck sand, and still I did not wake.  
The sea went on breathing in the dark,  
but I—  
I broke, and broke, and broke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an elegy in the style of an old English mourning poem, where a mother recounts her child’s death, funeral journey, emotional numbness, and longing to have him back “once more.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Once More**

I bore him beneath my breast,  
bright was the morning then;  
small was the hand that held me,  
soft was his breath in sleep.  
Now cold is the cradle-corner,  
quiet the little room;  
the wind goes under the door-stone  
and whispers his name to me.

I saw when the shadow took him.  
No sword was in that battle,  
no storm shook the roof-tree,  
no horn called men to war;  
yet death came over the threshold,  
dark-cloaked, patient, still,  
and laid one hand on his eyelids  
and one on the heart of me.

I called, but he did not answer.  
I kissed, but he did not wake.  
His curls lay fair on the linen,  
his mouth was a rose gone pale.  
The women wept around me;  
their wailing filled the walls.  
I sat as a stone in winter,  
hearing, yet hearing not.

Then we bore him from the homestead  
by the long and sorrowful way.  
The wheels went slow in the mire,  
the horses bowed their heads;  
the bell in the gray church-tower  
tolled like a heart far off.  
Fields lay bare beside us,  
and crows cried over the furrows.

I held no tear for the roadside,  
no cry for the staring sky.  
My hands were folded and empty,  
my face was white as wool.  
They said, “She is brave in sorrow,”  
but bravery was not mine;  
grief had frozen the wellspring,  
and numbness sat in my bones.

At the earth’s dark edge they lowered him,  
my little light, my lamb.  
The priest spoke words of heaven,  
of mercy, rest, and dawn;  
but I heard only the gravel  
falling, falling down—  
each clod a door between us,  
each sound a world away.

O child of my arms, my darling,  
where do your footfalls go?  
Do angels lift you laughing  
through meadows no frost can find?  
Do you remember your mother,  
her song at the fall of night,  
the warmth of her worn cloak round you,  
the beat of her heart nearby?

Give me one hour of morning,  
one breath against my cheek;  
let me smooth your hair from your forehead,  
let me hear your voice in the door.  
Though the graves be deep as winter,  
though the seas lie wide between,  
I would barter all my tomorrows  
to hold you once more—once more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
